seoTitle: Sore Throat and Airway Emergencies: McIsaac to Epiglottitis
metaDescription: Sore throat, stridor and nosebleeds in the ED, fork by fork: McIsaac and the strep test, epiglottitis, deep neck abscesses, croup, angioedema and packing.
h1: Sore throat, stridor and epistaxis: the ED algorithm, fork by fork
dek: For the student on an EM, ENT or pediatrics rotation with a sore throat, a stridulous child or a nosebleed and a resident about to ask what is next: the airway first, McIsaac and the strep test, deep neck abscesses, croup, angioedema, nasal packing, and the traps.

shortAnswer.text: Drooling, stridor, a tripod posture, a muffled voice, trismus or swelling under the jaw: keep the patient upright and calm and call the most skilled airway team. No throat exam, IV line or film in a child with suspected epiglottitis.

shortAnswer.lead: Pediatric epiglottitis goes to the operating room.
shortAnswer.text: Controlled intubation by anesthesia and ENT with a tracheostomy ready, then cultures and IV ceftriaxone or another third-generation cephalosporin. An adult not in extremis gets flexible nasolaryngoscopy by ENT, sitting up.

Centor plus 1 point at age 3 to 14 and minus 1 at 45 or older. 1 or less: no test, no antibiotic. 2 or more: a rapid strep test. One review tests adults only at Centor 3 or more, and NICE prescribes by score without a routine test.

shortAnswer.lead: Positive test: penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days (NICE: 5 to 10).
shortAnswer.text: Or one IM dose of benzathine penicillin G. A child with a negative rapid test gets a backup throat culture (one source says it may be done); adults do not.

shortAnswer.lead: Mono: test for EBV, and no amoxicillin.
shortAnswer.text: EBV-specific antibodies or a heterophile test, plus an HIV test; supportive care; no contact sports for at least 3 to 4 weeks.

shortAnswer.lead: Deep neck infection: CT neck with IV contrast once the airway is safe.
shortAnswer.text: Ludwig angina gets awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation with a surgical airway ready first. A peritonsillar abscess gets needle aspiration or incision and drainage, plus antibiotics; the sources disagree on whether every one needs draining.
0.6 mg/kg by mouth is the usual dose. Stridor at rest or a Westley score of 3 or more adds nebulized epinephrine and 3 to 4 hours of observation after the last dose.

shortAnswer.lead: Nosebleed: lean forward, pinch the soft nose for 10 to 15 minutes.
shortAnswer.text: Then a vasoconstrictor, cautery to one side of the septum only, anterior packing, and a posterior or double-balloon pack with admission when anterior measures fail.

sections.heading: What is the first step with drooling, stridor or a heavy nosebleed?
sections.intro: The airway, then the circulation. Keep the patient upright and calm, call anesthesia and ENT, and plan for failure, front-of-neck access included.

sections.heading: How do the first look, the scores and the scans sort a sore throat?
sections.intro: The forks read the airway picture, the throat and neck exam, the Westley and McIsaac scores, the rapid strep test, the CT, and the bleeding after each step.

sections.heading: Epiglottitis, mono or strep: who needs a strep test?
sections.intro: Nasolaryngoscopy for the adult with a muffled voice and a near-normal mouth, EBV testing for the mono picture, McIsaac for the rest, and bronchoscopy for a suspected inhaled foreign body.

sections.heading: How are strep throat, peritonsillar abscess, croup and epistaxis treated?
sections.intro: Antibiotics by diagnosis, drainage for an abscess, dexamethasone and epinephrine for croup, stopping the ACE inhibitor for angioedema, and pressure, cautery and packing for a nosebleed.

sections.heading: When do you get a CT for a sore throat or neck swelling?
sections.intro: For a suspected deep neck infection: CT neck with IV contrast once the airway is safe or secured, with an airway clinician present if it is at risk.

sections.heading: How is the rapid strep test done, and when is a backup culture needed?
sections.intro: Both tonsils and the posterior pharynx swabbed before any antibiotic; a child with a negative rapid test gets a backup throat culture, necessary in one source and optional in another.

sections.heading: Where does each throat and airway patient end up?
sections.intro: Every branch ends on a named diagnosis and its plan, from intensive care for epiglottitis to home after an hour of observation for a settled nosebleed.

items.text: Swollen, tender anterior cervical nodes: 1 point.
Age 3 to 14: plus 1. Age 15 to 44: 0. Age 45 or older: minus 1.
1 or less: no test and no antibiotic. 2 or more: rapid strep test.
Under 3: testing may be omitted unless a sibling has confirmed strep.

rounds.present: 8-year-old boy, 26 kg, with group A strep pharyngitis: 1 day of sore throat, fever to 38.9 and a stomachache, no cough or runny nose. Airway safe, with a normal voice and no drooling or stridor; no tonsillar bulge, neck supple, spleen not felt, so no abscess, neck or mono features. McIsaac 4 (tender anterior nodes, fever, no cough, age 3 to 14; no exudate), so a rapid antigen test, which is positive. Plan: penicillin V or amoxicillin by mouth for 10 days, acetaminophen or an NSAID, back to school after 24 hours of antibiotic, and reassess if he is not better within 5 days.

pimp.q: Why no lateral neck film in a child with suspected epiglottitis?
pimp.a: Imaging waits for the airway, and about 20% of lateral neck films miss it. It is a clinical diagnosis.

pimp.q: Exudative sore throat and a palpable spleen. Why not amoxicillin?
pimp.a: This is mono until tested: antibiotics are not indicated, and amoxicillin brings a maculopapular rash in up to 30%.

pimp.q: Why penicillin and not azithromycin for strep?
pimp.a: Penicillin is the only antibiotic shown to cut rheumatic fever, and no penicillin resistance has been documented. Macrolides are for penicillin allergy, with resistance widely documented.

pimp.q: Why not a beta-agonist nebulizer for croup?
pimp.a: Beta-agonists can worsen upper airway obstruction. Nebulized epinephrine is for stridor at rest or moderate to severe croup.

pimp.q: ACE inhibitor angioedema with stridor. Why not epinephrine, steroids and antihistamines first?
pimp.a: Bradykinin-mediated swelling often resists them, so the airway is secured early by an awake technique, surgical airway ready.

pimp.q: Why cauterize only one side of the septum?
pimp.a: Cauterizing both sides risks a perforation.

traps.text: Lying a drooling, stridulous patient flat to look at the throat. Upright and calm, no tongue blade, the airway team first.
A lateral neck film before the airway team in suspected epiglottitis. Imaging waits for the airway.
Calling a cough or runny nose proof of a virus. It makes strep less likely without ruling it out; the score decides the test.
Antistreptolysin O titers to diagnose strep throat. They reflect past infection; the rapid antigen test is the primary test.
Amoxicillin for mono. Antibiotics are not indicated, and amoxicillin brings a rash in up to 30%.
Switching ACE inhibitor angioedema to another ACE inhibitor. Every ACE inhibitor is contraindicated after it.
Abdominal thrusts for a child who is still coughing. She is left to cough; thrusts are for the child who cannot cough, speak or breathe, and a normal chest film does not exclude the foreign body.
Head tilted back for a nosebleed. Lean forward and pinch the soft nose, not the bony bridge.

faq.a: The Centor criteria plus an age adjustment: 1 point each for tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical nodes, absent cough and a temperature over 38 C (100.4 F), plus 1 at age 3 to 14 and minus 1 at 45 or older. A score of 1 or less needs no test; 2 or more gets a rapid strep test. At 15 to 44 it equals the Centor score.

faq.q: Who needs a rapid strep test?
faq.a: Anyone without abscess, neck or mono signs whose McIsaac (or Centor at 15 to 44) is 2 or more. The sources disagree for adults: the Acute Pharyngitis review tests adults at a Centor of 3 or more, and NICE does not recommend rapid tests routinely, prescribing by score instead. Testing may be omitted under 3 unless a sibling has confirmed strep.

faq.q: What is the treatment for strep throat?
faq.a: Penicillin V or amoxicillin by mouth for 10 days (NICE: 5 to 10 days), or one IM dose of benzathine penicillin G, with acetaminophen or an NSAID for pain. Without an immediate-type allergy, cephalexin or cefadroxil; after an immediate reaction, clindamycin or a macrolide. Back to school or work after 24 hours of antibiotic, and reassess if not better within 5 days.

faq.q: How is a peritonsillar abscess treated?
faq.a: Airway first if there is drooling, tripoding or labored breathing. Then needle aspiration or incision and drainage, sitting up with topical anesthetic, plus antibiotics such as clindamycin, ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate, with analgesia, IV fluids and a steroid to consider. Point-of-care ultrasound can confirm it, and the sources disagree on whether every abscess needs drainage.

faq.q: What is the dexamethasone dose for croup?
faq.a: One dose by mouth, 0.6 mg/kg being the usual one; 0.15 and 0.3 mg/kg appear equally effective. It goes IM or IV if the child cannot swallow, is vomiting or is in severe distress. Stridor at rest or a Westley score of 3 or more adds nebulized epinephrine, with 3 to 4 hours of observation after the last dose.

faq.q: How do you stop an anterior nosebleed?
faq.a: Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft, cartilaginous nose for 10 to 15 minutes. If it keeps bleeding, suction the clots and apply a topical vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline. A visible anterior point gets silver nitrate on one side of the septum only; otherwise anterior packing. Home after at least 1 hour of stable observation, with follow-up within a week.
